title: Lighthouse cache throttle RCA and recovery handoff
summary: Post-incident follow-up to walk through the cache-throttling regression that increased tail latency for the Lighthouse feed service. We confirmed a multi-factor root cause (client surge + batching regression + KV cache eviction interaction), agreed on short-term mitigations, and scheduled benchmarks and an ops playbook handoff.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-02 15:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Cole, Priya Raman, Liam Ortiz (Redwood) — Alex Moreno, Dana Wu, Samir Patel, Jill Kramer (Lighthouse)

Summary (auto): quick RCA walk, agree mitigations, assign owners.

[00:00] Ethan Cole: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on short notice. we wanted to walk through what happened last weekend with the feed ingestion — the KV cache throttling that pushed tail latencies up.
[00:14] Alex Moreno: yeah, thanks. appreciate you doing this. it was rough for us, customers saw a big spike in 95 and 99. we had pagers.
[00:22] Jill Kramer: just to set expectations — executive asked for timeline and what we put in place to stop it reoccurring.
[00:30] Priya Raman: quick preface — we've got preliminary traces and a reproducer. initial read shows three contributing factors: sudden client-driven QPS spike, a batching policy change that increased per-request token counts, and an interaction with our prefix/kv cache eviction logic that created hot-keys and thrashing.
[00:52] Dana Wu: can you expand on the kv cache part — our infra team saw many cache evicts and a lot of small rehydrates. is that the same?
[01:05] Priya Raman: yes, so our runtime keeps a small LRU-like KV cache for past prefixes. during high fanout the eviction rate shot up; the batching change meant requests were sending longer contexts so KV windows were bigger, causing more memory pressure and causing the runtime to fall back to recompute embeddings more often. that recompute path is heavier and increases per-request latency.
[01:32] Samir Patel: when you say batching policy change, is that something on Redwood side or client-side?
[01:36] Ethan Cole: that was a config tweak we rolled out in the serving tier two weeks ago — it was intended to improve throughput by grouping by similar seq-len, but under a sudden spike it created larger batches that delayed small quick requests. in hindsight the adaptive limit was too permissive for bursty workloads.
[01:58] Alex Moreno: sounds like a classic latency vs throughput tradeoff; we hit it because our analytic pipeline backfilled and sent lots of historical replays.
[02:08] Priya Raman: exactly. the replay created a mix of long and short sequences; larger batches wait on longer sequences; meanwhile KV cache didn't protect hot prefixes because the replays had varied tokens that reduced cache locality.
[02:24] Jill Kramer: any single point failure? can we blame a particular node pool?
[02:29] Priya Raman: we did see a subset of hosts on the egress tier with higher network queue depth, but not a total outage. more of an emergent tail effect across a few racks.
[02:39] Dana Wu: what about autoscaling? why didn't we scale fast enough?
[02:43] Liam Ortiz: autoscaling responded but the capacity had to remap KV shards which added churn; the cold migration cost added to tail. plus some of the pre-warmed nodes had different quantization kernels and were slightly slower.
[02:59] Alex Moreno: that remapping detail is new to us — can you point to logs?
[03:02] Priya Raman: we'll share the mapping logs. the important bit is that scale-up caused more KV evictions temporarily which amplified latency.
[03:12] Samir Patel: okay, so multi-factor. what are short term mitigations we can do right now?
[03:17] Ethan Cole: we proposed three immediate actions: 1) rollback the adaptive batching change for their dedicated pool (turn it off or enforce smaller max batch window), 2) pin KV cache reservations for Lighthouse customer shards to prevent eviction during scale events, 3) put an emergency rate-limit on backfills from their analytics pipeline while we run repros.
[03:38] Jill Kramer: is pinning shards safe? does it cause resource starvation?
[03:41] Priya Raman: it's safe as a temporary fix; it reduces flexibility in autoscaler but we can set a short TTL and monitor. we recommend 48-72 hour pin to get through initial checks.
[03:52] Dana Wu: are there risks to rolling back the batching change? any perf loss?
[03:55] Ethan Cole: you'll lose some throughput efficiency in steady-state, maybe 5-8% for that workload, but you'll reduce p99 spikes. it's an acceptable trade for an emergency.
[04:05] Alex Moreno: what about instrumentation — we need better signals so we can see when the system approaches the dangerous region.
[04:10] Priya Raman: agreed. we'll add new metrics: per-shard eviction rate, per-batch max-seq-len, and a batch-wait-time gauge. we'll provide Grafana panels and alert conditions.
[04:23] Jill Kramer: can you share which dashboards and who gets alerts? we need to include Lighthouse oncall and our platform eng.
[04:29] Liam Ortiz: will do. we'll add a dedicated dashboard and a runbook pointer.
[04:33] Ethan Cole: about SLA and credits — Ethan here — we discussed an emergency credit to offset customer impact. we want to propose a small usage credit and a pilot to test the pinned-shard strategy.
[04:46] Jill Kramer: send something written please, that'll make the execs happy.
[04:49] Ethan Cole: yes, will send today.
[04:52] Alex Moreno: on the repro side, can you reproduce end-to-end? seeing the mix of long and short sequences is key.
[04:58] Priya Raman: yes — we have a repro harness that simulates the replay pattern. first pass reproduces the latency climb at ~2x normal QPS; we'll run it again with kernel tracing to capture system-call and kernel scheduling queuing.
[05:14] Dana Wu: please also capture jemalloc stats and IO wait if possible. during the incident we saw small jitter correlated with gc-like events.
[05:23] Priya Raman: noted. we'll include allocator and io metrics.
[05:26] Samir Patel: long-term what are we changing?
[05:29] Priya Raman: roadmap items: better adaptive backoff for batching that considers per-customer burstiness, KV cache reservation APIs, improved shard remapping that avoids full eviction storms, and an admission-control layer that throttles non-critical replays under pressure.
[05:45] Alex Moreno: timeline for those?
[05:47] Priya Raman: short term (1 week) — rollback + pin + dashboards. medium (4-6 weeks) — safer batching policy + reservation API. longer (2-3 months) — admission control and remap algorithm rewrite.
[05:58] Jill Kramer: that sounds reasonable. we'll want checkpoints and metrics to show risk reduction.
[06:03] Ethan Cole: we'll include quantitative goals: target p99 reduction to pre-incident baseline within the rollback window and show that pinning avoids eviction spikes in repro.
[06:14] Alex Moreno: any security or compliance impacts from pinning shards? we have PCI considerations.
[06:18] Priya Raman: nothing new — data residency and encryption still apply; shard pinning is an ops configuration and doesn't change encryption or access controls. we'll document it for auditors.
[06:30] Dana Wu: ok please note the timelines in the runbook.
[06:33] Liam Ortiz: action owners we'll capture in the notes.
[06:36] Ethan Cole: open questions — do we want to run a controlled canary for rollback or just flip the flag on?
[06:42] Alex Moreno: prefer canary for 2 hours then broader. don't want surprises.
[06:46] Priya Raman: agree. we'll do a two-host canary in their dedicated pool, monitor, then widen.
[06:53] Jill Kramer: if the canary passes, what's the rollback-to-forward plan?
[06:57] Priya Raman: after canary passes we'll keep the old config as default for Lighthouse for 48-72 hours, then run a staged reintroduce with much stricter max batch window and extra alerts.
[07:09] Samir Patel: do you have mitigation scripts we can run from our side?
[07:12] Ethan Cole: yes, we can provide a small ops script to set rate-limits and shard pins; we'll put it in a shared repo with runbook steps.
[07:21] Alex Moreno: excellent. also want the raw logs so our SREs can correlate.
[07:25] Priya Raman: we'll share mapping logs, prometheus scrapes, and kernel traces once collected.
[07:31] Jill Kramer: final point — communications. we'll need a customer-facing postmortem. can Redwood help draft that?
[07:36] Ethan Cole: yes, we'll draft a customer-facing incident summary and share a technical appendix for your infra folks.
[07:42] Dana Wu: timeline for that doc?
[07:45] Ethan Cole: draft to you by EOD tomorrow, final after you review within 48 hours.
[07:50] Samir Patel: cool.
[07:52] Liam Ortiz: recap of immediate items: rollback canary, pin shards, run repro with traces, share scrapes/logs, draft credit and postmortem. owners listed in action items.
[08:06] Jill Kramer: thanks everyone. appreciate the responsiveness.
[08:10] Alex Moreno: thanks. we'll be watching alerts.
[08:13] Ethan Cole: thanks all. we'll follow up on email and schedule the handoff.

Transcript notes: transcription contains typical name mis-attributions (K-V cash, jemalloc typed as "jem alloc"), occasional ums/ahs removed for brevity, timestamps approximate every few minutes.

Attachments referenced: repro-harness link (internal), mapping-logs (will share link), proposed-credit-term-sheet (to be sent), runbook draft link (to be scheduled).
notes: This call was heavier on technical root cause than executive messaging. Redwood to own rollback canary & repro; Lighthouse to provide scrapes and runbook reviewers. Recommended immediate TTL pin of 72 hours and emergency credit draft.
